chunks: Some of them are like hocked camels,
some like butchered meat, some like severed limbs, some like spilt blood,
some are biting their hands, some are rubbing their palms, some are holding their cheeks on their hands,
some are cursing their own views and some are retreating from their determination.
But the time for action has gone away and the hour of calamity has approached,
(while there was no longer) the time to escape
Alas! Alas! What has been lost is lost! What has gone is gone!
The world has passed in its usual manner.
“So wept not on them the heavens and the earth nor were they respited.”
ai.seo_question: What does Nahj al-Balagha say about the state of those who missed their chance for salvation?
ai.summary: Imam Ali employs visceral imagery of slaughtered livestock to depict the irreversible finality of death for those who neglected their spiritual duties, a concept central to Shia eschatology regarding the 'Barzakh' or intermediate realm. The passage underscores the suddenness of the end of worldly opportunities, reinforcing the Shia scholarly emphasis on *Fana* (passing away) of the world and the urgency of *Tawbah* (repentance) before the soul is severed from the body.

en.sayed-ali-raza: Some of them are like hocked camel,
some like butchered meat, some like severed limbs, some like spilt blood,
some are biting their hands (in pain) some are rubbing their palms (in remorse), some are holding their cheeks on their hands (in anxiety),
some are cursing their own views and some are retreating from their determination.
But the time for action has gone away and the hour of calamity has approached,
while (there was no longer) the time to escape
(Qur’ān, 38:3). Alas! Alas! What has been lost is lost! What has gone is gone!
The world has passed in its usual manner.
“So wept not on them the heavens and the earth nor were they respited.” (Qur’ān, 44:29)
